source.title: Aligner: Efficient Alignment by Learning to Correct
source.authors: Jia-Ming Ji; Bo-Yuan Chen; Hantao Lou; Donghai Hong; Bo-Rong Zhang; Xue-Hai Pan; T. Qiu; Jun-Tao Dai; Yao-Dong Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly tests a weak-to-strong correction procedure: it fine-tunes stronger upstream models using answers produced by a smaller Aligner. This is a different procedure from directly fine-tuning on a weak model’s labels, and it reports outcome changes. It does not calculate PGR or compare the resulting student against the weak supervisor.
record.gate_note: Table 4 reports results for fine-tuning strong models on Aligner-produced corrections, so those outcomes are recorded. The paper does not report the weak Aligner’s evaluation scores or PGR, so the results cannot establish that a student beats its supervisor or recovers a fraction of the weak-to-strong gap. Other Aligner results, such as Table 1’s correction outcomes and the representation-control experiment, do not test the weak-to-strong fine-tuning claim. Cited results from Burns et al. are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Appendix A ('Weak-to-Strong Correction via Aligner') borrows the weak-to-strong framing. A small Aligner rewrites the strong model's own answers, and the strong model is then fine-tuned (SFT/RLHF/DPO) on those rewrites. The only measure is a GPT-4/human win rate of the fine-tuned model against its own original version (Eq. 5). The paper reports no score for the weak supervisor, no strong ceiling and no PGR. So it cannot show whether a student beats its weak supervisor (V1), whether a method raises PGR (V2), or how PGR scales (V3). It reports only its own procedure's improvement over the untrained upstream model. The supervisor is also not a standalone weak model but a weak corrector conditioned on strong outputs, a different construct from the original setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim Table 4 shows Aligner 'can achieve weak-to-strong generalization'. That claim rests only on gains over the original upstream model; they report no comparison with the weak supervisor and no PGR. They attribute the RLHF/DPO helpfulness drop to conservative response patterns, and say RLHF generally beats DPO in this semi-online setting.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of training a strong model directly on a weaker model’s standalone labels, the procedure has a smaller Aligner revise answers first generated by the strong upstream model; those corrections are then used as SFT targets or preferred answers for RLHF/DPO.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with student model size, training method and evaluation dataset; in particular, RLHF/DPO helpfulness changes differ from SFT and can be negative.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning 7B–70B models on corrections a smaller Aligner made to upstream answers raises win rates against the original model. SFT is positive everywhere (helpfulness +8.2% to +28.4% average). RLHF/DPO raise harmlessness but often lower helpfulness (e.g. Alpaca-7B DPO −51.3%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning a strong model on a smaller model's corrections of its outputs improves it relative to its original version, with helpfulness gains depending on the training method.

record.problems: The weak supervisor’s own scores and the student’s strong-model ceiling are not reported for this experiment, so supervisor-beating and PGR cannot be assessed. Table 4 reports percentage changes without uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: No comparison of the fine-tuned strong model with the weak Aligner (or with Aligner-corrected outputs); no PGR or strong ceiling.
SFT, RLHF and DPO are compared only on gain over the original model, not on PGR over naive weak-label fine-tuning.
Students of three sizes are trained, but there is no PGR and no systematic supervisor-size variation (Aligner-7B for 7B/13B students, Aligner-13B for 70B only).
No tests of supervisor exploitation, distribution shift or error similarity.
No theory on when a student beats its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation 'tests' and tranche T2 contradict its own finding that every version is untested; this verdict changes them to uses_without_test and T4. The main paper (Table 1, CAI comparison, multi-round RLHF, interpretability) is about inference-time correction and does not bear on the versions. Table 4 gives no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not compare the fine-tuned student with the weak supervisor or report PGR.
SFT, RLHF and DPO are compared for weak-to-strong correction, but the paper does not measure whether a change raises PGR over naive fine-tuning.
The paper varies student size, training method and evaluation dataset, but does not measure PGR or its dependence on supervisor/student size, task, or representations.
The paper does not test supervisor-checking failures, distribution-shift effects on PGR, or error similarity between weak and strong models.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested or derived.

rows.subject: Alpaca-7B
rows.operation_detail: SFT on labels produced by Aligner-7B
rows.baseline: original Alpaca-7B; numeric baseline not stated
rows.note: Reported as the change after weak-to-strong correction fine-tuning.
rows.check: Applies to all Table 4 rows. The measure is a win rate of the fine-tuned model vs the original upstream model, (Nw−Nl)/(Nw+Nl+Ne), not a percent change in a score. The baseline is the student's own pre-training version, not the weak supervisor. The Table 4 footnote says answers a come from Alpaca-7B for all students, which conflicts with the recipe description that the Aligner corrects each upstream model's own answers.
